stories.title: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant & Bar Inks Deal at 63 Cooper Square
stories.excerpt: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant & Bar is opening its fourth location in New York City and its fifth overall, Commercial Observer has learned. The growing Northern Chinese dining concept signed a 2,000-square-foot lease at 63 Cooper Square, an East Village property owned by Matthew Rettner, according to landlord broker Meridian Capital Group. Asking rent for the space was $21,600 per month, and the tenant signed a 15-year lease. The midblock site is one of several small commercial spots on the ground floor of a residential building along Third Avenue between St. Marks Place and East Seventh Street. “Cooper Square doesn’t have a ton of turnover, so when a turnkey restaurant space becomes available there, we want a tenant who can hit the ground running,” Meridian’s Daniel Zacaim said in a statement. “Dongbei’s operating history made this an easy recommendation to the landlord, and I think this location is going to perform very well for them.” Zacaim represented the landlord alongside Noam Aziz and Carson Shahrabani, while David Green and Benjamin Namdar of KSR negotiated on behalf of the tenant. The KSR brokers did not immediately respond to a request for comment. “What’s impressive about Dongbei is the consistency of their growth — four locations in New York plus a New Jersey expansion in the works,” Shahrabani said in a statement. “That kind of momentum makes landlords comfortable, and it made this negotiation move quickly and smoothly on both sides.” Dongbei has Manhattan locations at 953 Columbus Avenue on the Upper West Side, 367 West 36th Street in Midtown and 17 Ann Street in the Financial District, as well as a spot in Downtown Jersey City. Mark Hallum can be reached at mhallum@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant signs 2,000 sq ft lease at 63 Cooper Square, East Village Manhattan.
15-year lease at $21,600/month ($129.60/sq ft annually) signals strong retail confidence in Cooper Square.
Ground-floor retail activation in residential building reflects stable neighborhood demand and operator quality.
stories.summary: Dongbei Chinese Restaurant & Bar, a growing Northern Chinese dining concept, leased 2,000 square feet at 63 Cooper Square in Manhattan's East Village for $21,600/month on a 15-year term. The space, part of a mixed-use residential building on Third Avenue, was fully occupied at an asking rent of $129.60/sq ft annually. The landlord broker noted low turnover in the Cooper Square submarket and emphasized the tenant's proven operating history.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. Retail leasing velocity and rent growth in East Village signal neighborhood stability and consumer demand, which can support mixed-use or ground-floor retail in new residential projects, but this single lease does not move market fundamentals.

stories.title: Power Is No Longer an Input in Data Centers. It Is the Product.
stories.excerpt: A data center site can have land, fiber, approvals and a customer ready to deploy, and still be nearly worthless. The reason is changing what developers are actually searching for. Power scarcity is changing the economics of development. On power grid operator PJM, capacity prices jumped from $28.92 per megawatt-day for 2024-2025 to $269.92 for 2025-2026, then climbed again to $329.17 for 2026-2027. Power availability is increasingly becoming the asset around which everything else is assembled. Suhail Y Tayeb. PHOTO: Courtesy NYU Land and fiber still matter. But neither creates a viable project if electricity cannot arrive when the customer needs it. That changes the site-selection conversation. Where is the substation? How much capacity is actually available? When can the first tranche of power be delivered? A hyperscaler may ultimately need hundreds of megawatts, but not all on day one. If 50 megawatts can be energized now and another 100 can arrive 18 months later, that site may be more valuable than one promising 300 megawatts several years from now. Power is not valuable simply because it exists on a utility map. It is valuable when it can be delivered. That distinction is forcing developers deeper into the energy business. They are pursuing utility relationships, transmission access, substations and gas infrastructure with the same intensity they once reserved for land and entitlements. They are also confronting a mismatch in timelines. AI companies plan deployments in months. Major transmission projects, substations and generation assets can take much longer. The result is a growing market for solutions that bridge the gap. Behind-the-meter generation, co-generation and direct energy partnerships are increasingly part of the conversation. The question is no longer simply whether a utility can serve a project, but whether and how the developer can assemble an energy system until the grid catches up. bullets: PJM capacity prices surge from $28.92/MW-day (2024-25) to $329.17/MW-day (2026-27)—11x growth.
Power availability, not land or fiber, now determines data center project viability and site value.
Phased power delivery (50 MW now, 100 MW in 18 months) now more valuable than future larger capacity.
stories.summary: Power grid capacity has become the critical constraint in data center development, with PJM capacity prices climbing to $329.17 per megawatt-day for 2026-2027, up from $28.92 in 2024-2025. Developers can now possess land, fiber, approvals, and committed customers but still lack a viable project if electricity cannot be delivered when needed. The timing and tranche size of available power now matter more than the total future megawatt promise.
stories.impact: Profound implications for multifamily developers in power-constrained markets (Mid-Atlantic, Northeast). Data center competition for grid capacity will raise electricity costs and availability for residential projects, increasing operating expenses and potentially constraining new construction feasibility in dense urban/suburban nodes. Developers should lock in long-term power agreements early and avoid overbuilt markets; alternatively, this shifts demand back to secondary/tertiary metros with excess capacity or planned utility investment, creating new multifamily demand corridors outside legacy tech hubs.

stories.title: Anthony Cohen of Northmarq: 5 Questions
stories.excerpt: Northmarq’s Anthony Cohen is six years into his commercial real estate career and already holds top roles at a firm noted for its leasing, sales and debt acumen. Cohen, 34, is a managing director in Northmarq’s Los Angeles commercial investment sales office and co-leader of the firm’s national net-lease and sale-leaseback group. Since 2020 — when he started his real estate brokerage career at Ascension — Cohen has worked on deals with a cumulative volume exceeding $1 billion. His experience in both real estate and finance — he worked at J.P. Morgan for two years after college — make him a pro at advising businesses on their real estate needs. Cohen, who leads a team of five producers at Northmarq, said the most popular investment today is one that saves buyers money on taxes: accelerated depreciated assets like gas stations, car washes or even oil change sites. “Those are the most interesting and most highly sought-after assets right now,” he said. Commercial Observer sat down with Cohen last week to discuss that investment trend, his career so far, and what he’s seeing in the market today. This interview has been edited for length and clarity. Commercial Observer: Walk me through how you got started in real estate and where you were before Northmarq. Anthony Cohen: So I’m not too young, but not too old. I went to Penn State. I studied finance. My first job was at J.P. Morgan. I was working just outside of Philadelphia in Delaware, actually, and I was a financial analyst there, and, you know, did really well. Even though I got all the accolades of being a high performer, it’s very corporate, and upward mobility compensation is very hard to change. You just have to put in the hours and the years, and you’ll eventually be moving up the ladder. It was a really good experience to learn how to become a professional in the outside world, but I wanted something that had unlimited potential. Net-lease and sale-leaseback strategy shifts toward tax-efficient buys (gas stations, car washes, oil changes).

Cohen has worked on $1 billion-plus in deal volume since 2020, combining his real estate and finance (JPMorgan) background.
stories.impact: Signals capital market preference rotation away from multifamily toward single-tenant, tax-sheltered assets in lower-growth categories. This suggests institutional investor appetite for multifamily may be cooling or shifting to value-add/stabilized assets only; development capital is scarce and selective. Net-lease/sale-leaseback strength also indicates some operators are divesting real estate to raise liquidity, potentially freeing capital for acquisition but also increasing competitive selling pressure.

stories.title: Sunday Summary: Sharp Left
stories.excerpt: Summer’s done, and the hustle of fall will soon be upon us. Part of the background noise of the season will be the elections for state and federal legislatures. That includes the New York State Senate and Assembly. Those august Albany chambers are about to absorb a relatively large number of Democratic Socialists — and their allies — in the same vein as New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani. That could have serious ramifications for commercial real estate. We’re talking retail rent control; further restrictions on raising the rent on, or vacating, rent-stabilized apartments; and a much longer moratorium on the development of large-scale data centers. There’s also some potential good news in so many far-left pols heading up the Hudson at once: They have aggressive plans for fostering the development of much-needed affordable housing. Those plans should align with the commercial real estate industry’s own efforts (really). Otherwise, though, next year could bring regressive changes akin to the dreaded 2019 state housing legislation that followed lefty wins in the 2018 elections. Options can be a lifesaver Speaking of affordable housing, a niche financing option for the asset class is growing in popularity. It’s called tax-exempt commercial mortgage-backed securities (CMBS) debt. That debt can carry lower costs of capital than standard taxable CMBS or the affordable housing loans that Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac back. (For more on the state of CMBS, check out our Q&A with Trepp’s Stephen Buschbom and Andy Boettcher.) And, apropos of both legislatures and affordable housing, there’s a lot to recommend for the CRE industry in the recently enacted 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act. It’s the biggest single piece of federal housing legislation in decades, and it’s meant to foster a lot of new housing construction, particularly of the subsidized sort. Will it? bullets: Democratic Socialists gaining seats in NY State Senate and Assembly, similar to Mayor Mamdani.
Threats include retail rent control, stricter rent-stabilized apartment rules, and longer data center moratorium.
Opportunity: aggressive affordable housing development plans could align with CRE industry efforts.
stories.summary: New York State elections will bring a meaningful influx of Democratic Socialists and their allies to the state legislature, similar to the movement that elected Mayor Zohran Mamdani in NYC. This political shift could introduce restrictive policies including retail rent control, tighter restrictions on rent-stabilized apartments, and extended moratoriums on large-scale data center development. However, these legislators also have aggressive affordable housing development agendas that could align with commercial real estate industry interests.
stories.impact: HIGH STAKES FOR NY MULTIFAMILY. Stricter rent-stabilized regulations would materially constrain operating economics for rental properties serving middle-income tenants and reduce incentive for new supply. Retail rent control could undermine mixed-use project economics. Conversely, accelerated affordable housing incentives (zoning waivers, tax abatements, PILOT enhancements) could open new development windows for mission-driven or syndicated deals. Developers must prepare entitlement strategy now—some projects may become untenable under new rules; others could be fast-tracked with affordable components. Watch 2025 legislative calendar closely for rent control and data center moratorium language, which directly impact financing and valuation.

stories.title: Global Holdings Lands $382M Refi for Midtown Tower
stories.excerpt: Private equity firm Global Holdings has secured a $382.4 million refinancing loan for its Midtown Manhattan office tower at 120 Park Ave., with Wells Fargo and German bank LBBW originating the note. The funding, reported by The Real Deal, retires the property’s existing $335 million loan from HSBC. The recapitalization follows Bloomberg LP’s renewal in late 2025 of its 495,753-square-foot lease across 20 floors of the Class A building, marking one of the city’s largest lease deals of the year. Bloomberg’s lease, which was extended to 2024, accounts for roughly 80% of the property’s rentable area. Global Holdings acquired the 620,000-square-foot building neighboring Grand Central Terminal from Altria Group in 2008. The refinancing will facilitate a capital improvement program for the asset, which was built in 1981. Chaired by Eyal Ofer, Global Holdings has an international real estate portfolio spanning more than 10 million square feet of real estate, including 120 properties and over 1,500 hotel rooms. The post Global Holdings Lands $382M Refi for Midtown Tower appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Global Holdings refinances 120 Park Ave., Manhattan, for $382.4M (Wells Fargo, LBBW), up from $335M HSBC loan.
Bloomberg renewed 495,753 sq ft (20 floors, 80% of building) through 2024; one of largest NYC lease deals.
Class A office refi at strong valuation signals Manhattan institutional tenant stability and capital availability for trophy assets.
stories.summary: Global Holdings secured a $382.4 million refinancing for 120 Park Ave., a 620,000-square-foot Class A office tower in Midtown Manhattan, from Wells Fargo and German lender LBBW, retiring an existing $335 million HSBC loan. The refi was bolstered by Bloomberg LP's renewal of its 495,753-square-foot lease (20 floors, ~80% of rentable area) through 2024, representing one of NYC's largest lease transactions this year. Global Holdings acquired the 1981-built asset from Altria in 2008.
stories.impact: Demonstrates selective strength in Manhattan's Class A office sector for trophy assets with long-term anchor tenants (Bloomberg), but broader office market remains challenged. The willingness of institutional lenders to step in at higher proceeds suggests limited distress, at least for top-tier buildings with irreplaceable tenants. For multifamily developers, this signals persistent capital supply for blue-chip commercial assets but continued scarcity for speculative residential. No cascade effect on multifamily fundamentals in this transaction.

stories.title: NYC Plans 215-Unit Bronx Apartment Building
stories.excerpt: New York City’s Department of Housing Preservation & Development (HPD) has filed plans for a 215-unit apartment building on a vacant city-owned lot in the Bronx’s Melrose neighborhood. The 176,000-square-foot building at 3116–3124 Third Ave. would rise 20 stories, the New York Business Journal reported, citing plans filed with the New York City Planning Commission. HPD revealed that it has chosen Bronx-based developer Procida Cos. and community development nonprofit Nos Quedamos for the project. The building would also come with 7,000 square feet of commercial space and amenities including a community room, second-floor terrace and roof terrace. If realized, the project would advance the Melrose Commons Urban Renewal Plan, which proposes to bring new affordable housing across a 33-block area. To make way for the project, HPD is requesting that the city remove the 85-foot height limit for new multifamily developments in the vicinity. The department has also asked the Planning Commission create an Urban Development Action Area Program within the neighborhood that would set forth guidelines for developing income-restricted and affordable housing. The post NYC Plans 215-Unit Bronx Apartment Building appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: NYC HPD plans 215-unit affordable building at 3116–3124 Third Ave., Melrose, Bronx; 20 stories, 176k sq ft.
Developer Procida Cos. and nonprofit Nos Quedamos selected; includes 7k sq ft commercial space and roof terraces.
HPD seeks to remove 85-foot height limit and create Urban Development Action Area, enabling larger development scale.
stories.summary: New York City's Department of Housing Preservation & Development filed plans for a 215-unit affordable apartment building on Third Avenue in the Bronx's Melrose neighborhood, designed by Procida Cos. and Nos Quedamos. The 176,000-square-foot, 20-story building includes 7,000 square feet of commercial space and community amenities. HPD is requesting height limit increases and an Urban Development Action Area designation to facilitate affordable housing development across the 33-block Melrose Commons Urban Renewal Plan area.
stories.impact: SIGNIFICANT DEMAND SIGNAL FOR BRONX MULTIFAMILY. HPD's public investment in Melrose signals confidence in the submarket and de-risks entitlements for private developers; height waiver and UDAA zoning framework will facilitate future multifamily projects in the corridor. Procida's involvement (established Bronx-focused developer) indicates proven operating and community relationships. This pipeline addition (215 units) is modest in absolute terms but catalytic—expect private developers to queue projects for approval in the same zone within 12–24 months. Melrose has seen steady population stabilization and retail activation; this development should drive further residential investment in the Third Avenue/Melrose node. Monitor timeline for UDAA approval and any affordability covenants, which will set precedent for follow-on projects.

stories.title: Northern New Jersey Shopping Center Changes Hands
stories.excerpt: Adoni Property Group has acquired the 60,614-square-foot shopping center in Northern New Jersey’s Basking Ridge from Kushner Real Estate Group. JLL Capital Markets arranged the sale and secured $12.2 million in acquisition financing on behalf of the buyer through an unidentified life insurance firm. Built in 2000, the community retail center spans approximately 11 acres at 546 Allen Rd. and includes five buildings that were fully leased to 18 tenants at the time of the sale. Four new leases executed within the past 12 months point to continued momentum at the property. Anchored by Walgreens and United States Postal Service locations, the shopping center sits within the master-planned community The Hills at Basking Ridge. “Highlands Village is a premier, necessity-based retail center with a proven history of stability and long-term tenant loyalty,” said Sonny Adoni, founder and CEO of Adoni Property Group in a statement. Westfield, NJ-based Adoni develops and manages a diversified portfolio of residential and commercial properties. Headquartered in Jersey City, Kushner Real Estate Group is a real estate investment and management firm with a portfolio of apartments and commercial space across four states. The post Northern New Jersey Shopping Center Changes Hands appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Adoni Property Group acquired 60,614 sq ft shopping center in Basking Ridge, Northern NJ, from Kushner REG.
JLL arranged $12.2M acquisition financing from life insurance firm; center fully leased with 18 tenants, 4 new leases in past 12 months.
Anchored by Walgreens and USPS; built 2000, situated in master-planned community The Hills at Basking Ridge.
stories.summary: Adoni Property Group acquired a fully-leased, 60,614-square-foot retail shopping center in Basking Ridge, Northern New Jersey, from Kushner Real Estate Group. JLL Capital Markets secured $12.2 million in acquisition financing from a life insurance firm. The center, built in 2000 and anchored by Walgreens and USPS, comprises five buildings and 18 tenants; four new leases were signed within the past 12 months, indicating continued momentum.
stories.impact: Minimal direct impact on multifamily development. Retail stability and lease momentum in the Basking Ridge masterplanned community (suburban New Jersey, near commute corridors) suggest stable suburban consumer demand and anchor tenant commitment. However, retail acquisition activity does not drive residential development unless part of mixed-use project pipeline. Note: Kushner REG's sale may signal portfolio optimization/capital redeployment, but no indication of multifamily impact.

stories.title: Iconic Rancho Cordova Furniture Showroom Listed for Sale
stories.excerpt: The longtime Rancho Cordova showroom of Beck’s Furniture has been listed for sale. The 208,800-square-foot property at 11840 Folsom Blvd has served primarily as a warehouse and distribution center for Beck’s Furniture, where people came to view the chairs and sofas before buying. The company closed its doors last year. The 10 acres along the Highway 50 corridor and has served as one of Northern California’s most recognizable furniture destinations for nearly 50 years. It features an approximately 90,000 square feet of showroom space and 120,000 square feet of warehouse and distribution space. Morrow Botros, Bryce MacDonald and Jay Hamer of Cushman & Wakefield have been exclusively retained to market the asset on behalf of the seller, Beck’s Furniture & Sleep / Beckinger Family Ownership.  Botros added, “For nearly 50 years, the Beck’s Furniture campus has stood as one of the Sacramento region’s most recognizable commercial landmarks. Few properties can claim both institutional scale and deep community recognition.” The post Iconic Rancho Cordova Furniture Showroom Listed for Sale appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Beck's Furniture showroom, Rancho Cordova CA (208,800 sq ft, 10 acres), listed for sale after company closure.
Property includes 90k sq ft showroom and 120k sq ft warehouse/distribution; operated 50 years on Highway 50.
Cushman & Wakefield exclusively marketing; iconic regional commercial landmark now available for repositioning.
stories.summary: The Beck's Furniture showroom and distribution campus in Rancho Cordova, California—a 208,800-square-foot, 10-acre property on the Highway 50 corridor—has been listed for sale following the company's closure last year. The facility includes approximately 90,000 square feet of showroom and 120,000 square feet of warehouse/distribution space. It served as a recognizable Northern California retail destination for nearly 50 years. Cushman & Wakefield is exclusively marketing the asset.
stories.impact: POTENTIAL MULTIFAMILY REDEVELOPMENT OPPORTUNITY IN SACRAMENTO METRO. Beck's Furniture closure and 10-acre Highway 50 frontage in Rancho Cordova (suburb east of Sacramento) represent a significant infill redevelopment site. Highway 50 is a major regional commute and economic corridor. Land area, existing visibility, and infrastructure access make the site viable for mixed-use (retail + multifamily) or residential-only development, particularly given Sacramento's affordable housing demand and regional job growth (state capital, tech inflow from Silicon Valley). Developers should monitor sale process; Sacramento County/Rancho Cordova entitlements are relatively streamlined. Site could support 300–600+ units if zoned/approved for residential; strong value-creation opportunity if acquired at reasonable basis relative to commercial salvage value.

stories.title: Tishman Speyer Trades Mountain View Office Building for $121.5M
stories.excerpt: Tishman Speyer sold 400 Castro Street, a 100 percent leased, Class A office building in downtown Mountain View, California. Spear Street Capital was the buyer in the $121.5 million transaction. Tishman Speyer developed the 138,000-square-foot property in 2002 and immediately leased the office space in full to Fenwick & West, which has remained a customer in the building. Tishman Speyer claims the transaction represents one of the strongest pricing outcomes for a Mountain View office sale in recent years. Centrally located with convenient access to highways and Caltrain, 400 Castro features expansive roof decks, underground parking and views of the San Francisco Bay and coastal mountains. The property, which was 100% leased at the time of the sale, is located in the heart of Downtown Mountain View, surrounded by restaurants and retail, with Cascal restaurant, Peet’s Coffee, and Sweetgreen on site. Tishman Speyer was represented by the Eastdil Secured team led by Nate Jones. The post Tishman Speyer Trades Mountain View Office Building for $121.5M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Tishman Speyer sold 400 Castro Street, Mountain View office, to Spear Street Capital for $121.5M.
138,000 sq ft Class A building, fully leased to Fenwick & West law firm since 2002 development.
Tishman claims 'strongest pricing outcome for Mountain View office sale in recent years' despite office sector headwinds.
stories.summary: Tishman Speyer sold 400 Castro Street, a 138,000-square-foot, 100%-leased Class A office building in downtown Mountain View, California, to Spear Street Capital for $121.5 million. The property, developed by Tishman in 2002, has been fully occupied by law firm Fenwick & West since opening. Tishman characterized the transaction as representing one of the strongest pricing outcomes for a Mountain View office sale in recent years.
stories.impact: Signals selective strength in Bay Area/Silicon Valley trophy office with fortress tenancy, but not indicative of broad multifamily dynamics. Spear Street's acquisition at reported peak pricing suggests stable institutional capital still seeking core+ office in tech-dominant markets, particularly with irreplaceable tenants (top law firms). For multifamily developers: Mountain View office strength does not translate to residential demand; in fact, office market bifurcation (trophy vs. distressed) suggests capital remains scarce for speculative multifamily. Bay Area multifamily development remains supply-constrained and capital-intensive; this office transaction does not alter that calculus.

stories.title: Related Secures $65M Refi for Office Property in L.A.’s South Bay
stories.excerpt: The owners of a 301,000-square-foot Class A office property in Los Angeles’ South Bay have secured refinancing for the property. Owners Related Companies and Cruzan landed the $64.7 million loan from Waterfall Asset Management and Delaware Life for the eight-story property called the Torrance, named after its home city. The asset at 21250 Hawthorne Boulevard is 93 percent occupied, according to Yardi Matrix, with tenants including All Nippon Airways, Salon Republic, Barrister Executive Suites, Compass California, Unio Health Partners and Morgan Stanley. Newmark’s Jordan Roeschlaub, Nick Scribani and Chris Lozinak arranged the debt. The property was built in 1988. Related and Cruzan acquired it from Stream Realty Partners for $106.8 million in 2017, and secured $59.2 million in refinancing in 2022. The South Bay has benefited from surging demand from aerospace and defense users for both office and industrial space. But the Greater Los Angeles office market remains deeply bifurcated. Overall vacancy was at 25.3 percent after the second quarter, nearly unchanged from year-end 2025, while trophy properties have a 13.5 percent vacancy rate, according to Newmark research. Gregory Cornfield can be reached at gcornfield@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Related and Cruzan refinanced 301,000 sq ft Torrance office for $64.7M (Waterfall, Delaware Life).
Eight-story property at 21250 Hawthorne Boulevard, 93% occupied; tenants include ANA, Morgan Stanley, Barrister Suites.
South Bay office benefits from aerospace/defense demand; LA market remains bifurcated between trophy and distressed assets.
stories.summary: Related Companies and Cruzan secured a $64.7 million refinancing from Waterfall Asset Management and Delaware Life for the Torrance, a 301,000-square-foot Class A office property in Los Angeles' South Bay at 21250 Hawthorne Boulevard. The 1988-built, eight-story property is 93% occupied with tenants including All Nippon Airways, Morgan Stanley, Compass California, and Barrister Executive Suites. Related and Cruzan acquired the asset from Stream Realty Partners for $106.8 million in 2017 and last refinanced for $59.2 million in 2022.
stories.impact: South Bay office strength (aerospace/defense tenant demand) does not extend to multifamily. Refinancing at stable LTV/basis reflects selective lender appetite for stabilized, credit-worthy office but masks broader LA bifurcation. For multifamily developers in Southern California: South Bay industrial and office uptake is driven by specialized tenants (defense contractors, aerospace); residential demand follows but lags. LA multifamily market overall remains capital-constrained and delivery-heavy; focus on secondary/tertiary metros or value-add/adaptive reuse rather than land development. Aerospace/defense growth could support modest rental demand for South Bay workforce housing (Torrance, Manhattan Beach, Redondo Beach submarkets) but does not alter capital scarcity or development feasibility.
